volumes.title: What the Basket Holds
volumes.text:
I am Marnie Tuck, mender, of number four Thimble Row in Emberwick. I do not make new things. There are dressmakers for that, and good luck to them. I put right what is torn, worn, burnt, outgrown or sat upon.

By my door stands a willow basket the size of a washtub. The rule is painted on the lid: pin a ticket to it, with your name and what is wrong. People leave things on their way to work and call back on Saturday. I shall keep this book for one year, January to December, and set down what the basket holds each month and whose it was.

It begins oddly. This morning, under two aprons, I found a fisherman’s jersey, dark blue, with the left elbow torn clean out. No ticket. No name. I have put it at the bottom until somebody owns up.

volumes.title: The Baker’s Third Pocket
volumes.text:
February in the mending basket at Thimble Row, and I, Marnie Tuck, have Osric Fenn’s apron again. Mr. Fenn bakes the town’s bread and keeps his mind on it. Everything else goes in his apron pocket, including, this week, a tray cloth straight from the oven door. That is the third pocket burnt through since harvest.

I have lined the new one with mattress ticking, doubled, and told him it will stand anything short of an actual loaf tin. He looked thoughtful. I should not have mentioned the loaf tin.

The blue jersey with no ticket is still at the bottom of the basket. Nobody has asked for it. On Tuesday I had a fire, an idle hour, and a hole in an elbow, which is an irritating thing to sit near. I have picked up the stitches around the edge. That is all.

volumes.title: A Coat Cut Down
volumes.text:
March. I am Marnie Tuck, the mender on Thimble Row, and this month the basket by my door was too small for the job. Mrs. Ida Larch carried it in over her arm instead: her late husband’s brown overcoat, to be cut down for their grandson Wilf, who is seven and has gone through the elbows of everything he owns.

She asked to stay while I marked it with chalk. When I picked up the shears she remembered an errand at the chandler’s. I waited until the bell had stopped swinging before I cut.

It made a good small coat, with enough hem turned up to see Wilf through two winters. In the inside pocket I found a stub of carpenter’s pencil. I sewed the pocket into the new coat exactly where it had been and put the pencil back. Mrs. Larch did not ask, and I did not say.

volumes.title: The Constable’s Misfortune
volumes.text:
April, and a parcel in my mending basket that was not there at closing time. I am Marnie Tuck of Thimble Row, and I know brown paper tied by a man in a hurry when I see it. Inside: one pair of uniform trousers, split along the seat from stem to stern. The ticket said only “B.T. Urgent. Please.”

Constable Bram Tolley came for them after dark, by the back door. It had been the miller’s gander, he said. It had got into the Corn Hall, and he had bent to reason with it.

I had put in a double seam and a gusset, since a constable must be able to bend. He paid at once and asked whether the nature of the repair need be known. I said a mender is like a doctor. The gander is bound by no such rule, and has been seen looking pleased.

volumes.title: Names Along the Hem
volumes.text:
May brought the Sedge family’s christening gown to my basket at Thimble Row, wrapped in a pillowcase and carried four miles in from the marsh. I am Marnie Tuck. I mend, mostly, but once in a generation I am asked to add.

The gown is fine lawn, soft as a moth. Around the hem, in white thread on white, runs the name of every baby who has worn it: Josiah, Hepzibah, Tom, another Tom, Ruth. I counted nineteen. The new one is Clover. I worked her in after Ruth, in the same small backstitch, with room left beyond her.

One name, I noticed, had been unpicked and stitched again. The old needle holes show if you tilt the cloth. It was Katharine once, with a K, and is now Catherine. Somebody felt strongly. I left it exactly as I found it. A mender does not take sides in a hem.

volumes.title: The Boy at the Window
volumes.text:
June, and I must put down something about the blue jersey. I am Marnie Tuck, mender, of Thimble Row, and that jersey has lain at the bottom of my basket since January with its elbow out and no ticket on it. I have been mending it in odd half hours, because nobody else will. The elbow is knitted in again. This week, turning up the hem, I found two letters worked into the rib: E.A. That is a Grey Coast habit, so that a jersey left on a quay goes home to the right man.

I know of no E.A. in Emberwick.

But there is a boy. Nine or so, hair like a hayrick. Three mornings this month he has stood at my window looking at the basket, not at me. Each time I reached the door, the lane was empty. He is quick. I am patient.

volumes.title: The Scarecrow’s Sunday Best
volumes.text:
July at Thimble Row. Six children from the Lowlands school filled my shop on Monday, all talking, carrying between them a coat that had plainly spent the winter outdoors. I am Marnie Tuck, mender, and I asked for the ticket. The smallest girl produced it. It read: “Old Barnaby. Coat. Everything.”

Old Barnaby stands in Farmer Roke’s bean field with a turnip for a head. Rooks had been sitting on his shoulders quite unafraid, the children said, and it was shaming him.

I do not mend by halves, whoever the customer is. I patched both shoulders in red flannel, which rooks dislike, sewed back the collar, and added four brass buttons from the tin, because a scarecrow with buttons stands straighter. The children paid in broad beans. On Sunday I walked out past the field. Not a rook. Barnaby had his arms out as though about to make a speech.

volumes.title: Half a Lion
volumes.text:
August. The travelling players have set up in the Corn Hall, and on Wednesday their lion came to my shop on Thimble Row. I am Marnie Tuck, and I have mended most things, but not, until now, a lion.

His tail hung by three threads. The moth had been at his mane. The man inside him, a small mild person called Mr. Hobb, explained that there was a performance at seven and no second lion. So I mended the top half while he sat by my stove in the bottom half, drinking tea, with his furry feet crossed.

I sewed the tail on with waxed button thread and a square of canvas behind, and told him he could be swung by it now if the play required. He said, rather wistfully, that he had only the one line. I went on Friday. He roared it beautifully, and the tail held.

volumes.title: Fourpence and a Name
volumes.text:
September, and the boy came in. I am Marnie Tuck, mender, of Thimble Row, and since January a blue fisherman’s jersey has sat in my basket without a ticket. Now I have the ticket’s worth by word of mouth.

He is Col Ashby, aged nine. The jersey is his father’s spare. His father is Edrin Ashby, who works the herring boats out of Saltgate on the Grey Coast and comes home at midwinter. Col wore the jersey up the schoolhouse apple tree last winter, to feel what it was like, and came down without the elbow. He had no money, so he left no name.

He put down fourpence and asked how much of an elbow that would buy. I said the price was fourpence and Saturday mornings, sorting my button tin, until the work was paid off. He shook hands on it like a man selling a horse.

volumes.title: The Left Sock
volumes.text:
October on Thimble Row. I am Marnie Tuck, mender, and on Saturdays I now have an assistant: Col Ashby, aged nine, who is working off the cost of a jersey elbow. He has sorted my button tin into shirt, coat, boot and “interesting”. The interesting pile is the largest.

This month he asked to learn darning. Mr. Gant the lamplighter had left a pair of grey socks in the basket, and I gave Col the left one, a wooden mushroom, and a needle. He wove over and under for an hour with his tongue between his teeth. The result was sturdy, and about the shape of a small potato.

I showed it to Mr. Gant honestly, beside my own. He turned Col’s over twice and said he would take it; his left foot had never been particular. Col walked home a clear inch taller, by my measure.

volumes.title: Weather from the Coast
volumes.text:
November. A gale came in off the Grey Coast on the ninth and blew for three days, and I, Marnie Tuck, mender, of Thimble Row, had a very quiet boy in my shop that Saturday. Col Ashby’s father is out with the Saltgate herring boats. News from the coast takes four days by the carrier.

I did not tell him not to worry. I got down the blue jersey, his father’s, the one we have been mending all year, and said the cuffs were fraying and I wanted them knitted afresh before midwinter. We unravelled them together. I picked up the stitches, and then I put the needles in his hands.

He knitted eleven rounds that morning, tight as a drum. On Wednesday the carrier called from his cart that every Saltgate boat was in. Col’s eleven rounds are still in the left cuff. I have not loosened them.

volumes.title: Paid in Full
volumes.text:
December, and the last page of my year. I am Marnie Tuck, mender, of Thimble Row. On the twentieth a broad man in a salt-stained cap came in, with Col Ashby pulling him by the sleeve. Edrin Ashby was home from the herring boats, and had come for his jersey.

He turned it over in his big hands. He found the new elbow, and the tight left cuff, and asked what he owed. I showed him the account: fourpence, and thirteen Saturday mornings, received with thanks. He looked at his son for some time. Then he said he was glad the mend showed. It meant somebody had minded.

They went up the lane with the jersey on him and Col tucked under one arm of it. Tonight the basket is empty, for the first time since January. It will not last, and I should be sorry if it did.

volumes.title: In and Out
volumes.text:
This is a book of stitches, one to a lesson, by Odile Farrow, who has taught the Thursday sewing class above Varley the chandler’s in Emberwick for twenty-six years. You will need a square of linen, a blunt needle, and patience. I can supply the first two.

Lesson one is running stitch. Bring the needle up, go forward the width of a barley grain, and go down. Come up again the same distance on. In and out, each stitch as long as the gap beside it. Everything else in sewing is this stitch with ideas above itself.

Two pupils began this January. Tansy Wickett is ten and finished her row before I had finished explaining it. Bertram Loach is fifty-three, works the ferry on the Ember, and wants to make a sampler for his mother’s ninetieth birthday in December. His row took the hour. It was straighter than Tansy’s.

volumes.title: One Step Back
volumes.text:
Lesson two, backstitch. I am Odile Farrow, and I teach sewing on Thursdays above the chandler’s in Emberwick. Backstitch is for anything that must be a solid line: a seam, a stem, a letter. Bring the needle up one stitch ahead of where you finished. Go back and down into the end of the last stitch. Come up one stitch ahead again. You travel forward by going backward, which my older pupils say is also how they get through a week.

My ferryman, Bertram Loach, has hands made for oars. The needle vanishes in them. Each time his thread came out of the eye he looked at it as a man looks for a dropped sixpence in long grass.

Tansy Wickett, ten, watched this three times. Then she took his needle, threaded it, and handed it back. He said, “Much obliged, miss.” They have shared a bench since.

volumes.title: Every Cross the Same Way
volumes.text:
Lesson three, from Odile Farrow’s Thursday class above the chandler’s in Emberwick: cross stitch. Linen is woven in a grid, and cross stitch sits on it like a mark on squared paper. Make one slanting stitch, bottom left to top right. Cross it with another, bottom right to top left. The one rule is that every top arm must slant the same way. Break it and the light catches each cross differently, and your work looks ruffled, like a cat stroked backwards.

A sampler begins with its alphabet, so this month the letters went on. Tansy Wickett, ten, reached G in an evening.

Bertram Loach, the ferryman, who is stitching a sampler for his mother’s ninetieth birthday, made one capital A. It took three Thursdays. Every arm lies the same way. He carried it round the room to show each of us in turn, and nobody minded in the least.

volumes.title: The Honest Unpick
volumes.text:
Lesson four is not a stitch. I am Odile Farrow, I have taught sewing in Emberwick for twenty-six years, and I say the most useful thing a needle does is go backwards. When a row is wrong, unpick it. Use the eye of the needle, not the point, so that you lift the thread and do not split it. Go one stitch at a time. Never pull.

Tansy Wickett, who is ten and quick, does not hold with this. She would rather sew a flower over a mistake and call it a garden.

Then Bertram Loach, my ferryman, found that the whole second line of his alphabet, H to P, sat one thread lower than the first. Nine letters, a month’s work. Then he turned his needle round and began. Tansy watched him as far as the K, sighed like a kettle, and started unpicking her garden.

volumes.title: Filling the Ferry
volumes.text:
Lesson five in this book of stitches is satin stitch, and I, Odile Farrow, warn you that it shows everything. It is for filling a shape with colour. Lay straight stitches side by side, so close no linen shows between, each one right across the shape. Do not pull them tight, or the cloth puckers like a mouth tasting a lemon. Let the thread lie.

Below his alphabet my ferryman pupil, Bertram Loach, has drawn his own boat, flat-bottomed, with the rope and the pole. He is filling her in brown.

The Thursday class had opinions. Tansy Wickett, ten, said the real ferry is more green than brown, from weed. Mr. Loach said this was his mother’s birthday sampler and the ferry would be shown as she ought to be. The hull took him all of May, and it lies as flat as the Ember on a still morning.

volumes.title: A River in Chain
volumes.text:
Lesson six, chain stitch. Bring the needle up, then put it back down in the same hole, leaving a loop on the surface. Come up a stitch farther on, inside the loop, and pull gently. Each link is held by the one after it. It makes a soft line, good for rope, vines and water.

I am Odile Farrow, of the Thursday class in Emberwick, and this June my pupil Bertram Loach ran the river Ember in blue chain across his sampler, under his brown ferry. While he worked he told us why he is making it.

His mother, Agnes Loach, kept the dame school at Ferry End for forty years. Every child stitched a sampler there. Her own she gave away, to a girl leaving for the Grey Coast with nothing to take. She has taught half the town its letters, and has none on her wall.

volumes.title: Eleven Lost Knots
volumes.text:
Lesson seven is the seed knot, and I, Odile Farrow, have seen it reduce grown pupils to silence. Bring the needle up. Wind the thread twice round it. Keep it taut with your other hand and put the needle down beside where it came up, not into the same hole. Draw it through slowly. A firm bead sits on the linen. Use the same hole, and the knot follows the needle through and is never seen again.

Bertram Loach, the ferryman, wanted stars above the boat on his mother’s sampler. He lost eleven knots through the cloth in one evening. I counted them by the sound he made.

Tansy Wickett, ten, got hers right at the first try and said so, several times. Mr. Loach bore it. Then he asked her to show him where his left hand should be. She did. There are seven stars over the ferry.

volumes.title: Stitching Between Crossings
volumes.text:
Lesson eight is stem stitch, for anything that bends. Work from left to right. Take a small stitch backwards along your line and bring the needle up halfway along the stitch before. Keep the thread always below the needle, never above. The stitches overlap like a twist of cord and will follow any curve.

I am Odile Farrow, and my Thursday class above the chandler’s does not meet in August. So Bertram Loach, who is sewing a sampler for his mother’s ninetieth birthday, took his reeds to work. He stitched them along the river bank on the cloth while sitting beside the real one, between crossings of his ferry.

His passengers helped. A farmer told him the reeds leaned the wrong way for the wind. A lady from the Lowlands said green was unlucky. Mr. Loach thanked them, charged them a penny each for the crossing, and changed nothing.

volumes.title: Where the Corners Meet
volumes.text:
Lesson nine in Odile Farrow’s book is herringbone, and with it, the border. Rule two faint lines. Take a small stitch on the top line, then a small stitch on the bottom line a little farther on, back and forth, until the long threads cross each other in a row of slanting legs. It looks like a fish’s backbone, or a fence drawn by somebody in a hurry.

A border must go round four sides and meet itself, so count the threads before you start. My ferryman, Bertram Loach, counted. At the last corner of his mother’s sampler the herringbone still arrived half a stitch early.

Tansy Wickett, who is ten and finished her own sampler in July, said, “Put a flower on it.” She looked at me, and I am afraid I nodded. Some gaps are not mistakes, only arithmetic. A flower gives a corner something to do.

volumes.title: A Damp Secret
volumes.text:
Lesson ten, blanket stitch, is for edges. Bring the needle up on the edge of the cloth. Go down a little way in, and come out at the edge again with the thread looped behind the needle. Pull, and a bar lies along the rim. Repeat evenly and no edge will fray.

I am Odile Farrow, sewing teacher of Emberwick, and in October my ferryman, Bertram Loach, was edging the secret sampler for his mother’s ninetieth birthday. Then his mother came down to the landing with his dinner. He pushed the sampler under the ferry seat. It stayed there through two crossings and a shower.

He brought it to class like a man carrying a drowned kitten. So, a second lesson. Lay damp work face down on a towel and press the back with a warm iron. The stitches sink into the towel and come up proud. His did.

volumes.title: Words for the Middle
volumes.text:
Lesson eleven. Every sampler carries some words, and I, Odile Farrow, have stitched and taught a great many that I should not care to live with: verses about duty, and early rising. Choose words you would be glad to read every day for forty years. Space them out on paper first, then work them in backstitch.

Bertram Loach, the ferryman, thought about his mother’s birthday sampler for two Thursdays. Then he wrote down what Agnes Loach said at the door of her dame school at Ferry End, every afternoon, to every child: “Mind the step. Come back tomorrow.”

He stitched it under the river in dark red, with his name and the year beneath. It was Tansy Wickett, ten, who saw that the N in “Mind” faced the wrong way. This was the first Thursday in December, with no time to unpick. I told him to let it be.

volumes.title: Fastening Off
volumes.text:
The last lesson is how to finish. Never end with a knot. Turn the work over, run the needle under four or five stitches, and snip close. The stitches hold it, and the back stays as honest as the front.

I am Odile Farrow, sewing teacher, and on her ninetieth birthday I went with my pupil Bertram Loach, the ferryman, to his mother’s kitchen at Ferry End. Tansy Wickett came to carry the parcel. Agnes Loach put on her spectacles and read the sampler slowly: alphabet, stars, ferry, river, reeds. At the words she stopped. “Bertram,” she said, “your N is backwards. It always was.” Then she asked him to hang it where she could see it from her chair.

It hangs there now. Tansy begins in January as my assistant. I close this book as I would a seam: under a few stitches, and no knot.

volumes.title: Twelve Iron Beds
volumes.text:
On the first Tuesday of February the schoolmaster of Emberwick, Mr. Alder Finch, stood up in the Corn Hall and explained about Brindle House. The old toll house by the bridge was to be made a winter lodging. Twelve children from the Northern Fells, who missed half their schooling whenever snow shut the high roads, would board there from November. The infirmary had given twelve iron beds. There were, as yet, no bedcovers.

Mrs. Dorcas Pimm, the draper’s widow, was on her feet before he had sat down. “A quilt for every bed,” she said. “The Tuesday Thimbles will see to it.”

The hall applauded. Dorcas sat, and only then counted the Tuesday Thimbles on her fingers. Herself. Old Hetty Marlow. The two Miss Vosses, who were not speaking. Ned Sorrel, the saddler’s boy. Five quilters, twelve quilts, nine months. She decided not to do the sum aloud.

volumes.title: Thirty Years of Dresses
volumes.text:
The first of the twelve quilts for Brindle House, where the fell children were to lodge, was begun by Dorcas Pimm on her own kitchen table in Emberwick. She had promised a quilt for every bed. It seemed only fair to start with her own scrap bag.

The bag held a snippet of every dress she had made in thirty years as the draper’s wife. Out came the green sprig from her sister’s wedding, a mourning grey, a yellow check from a summer she could no longer place. She cut them into oblongs and set them climbing corner to corner across the table, a pattern her mother had called Ember Steps.

It took all of March and every inch of her yellow thread. She spread it over the kitchen chairs and walked round it twice. Then she chalked a figure on the slate by the door: eleven.

volumes.title: Hetty’s Long Stitches
volumes.text:
The Tuesday Thimbles of Emberwick had promised twelve quilts for the twelve beds at Brindle House, and the second was Hetty Marlow’s. Hetty was eighty-one. She had quilted since she was six and saw little now, so she worked by touch, in plain squares of blue and cream, nine to a block. She called it Nine Windows.

Her stitches were enormous. A beetle could have walked under them. The two Miss Vosses exchanged the only look they had shared all year, and Prudence Voss murmured that perhaps, after Hetty went home, somebody might go over it.

Dorcas Pimm said no. She ran her hand across the quilt with her eyes shut. Every stitch stood up under her fingers like a row of small knuckles. “Some child,” she said, “will wake in the dark in a strange house. That child will be able to find this.” Nobody went over it.

volumes.title: Stitched to Hold a Horse
volumes.text:
Ned Sorrel was fifteen, apprenticed to the saddler in Emberwick, and the only one of the Tuesday Thimbles who had joined by accident. He had come to deliver a strap and been handed a needle. Now the circle owed twelve quilts to the twelve beds at Brindle House, and the third was his.

He had no scrap bag, so he begged flour sacks from the mill and feed sacks from the corn merchant, washed them soft, and pieced them in stripes of white and oat-brown. He sewed as he sewed harness, with two needles and waxed thread, every stitch pulled down hard.

Mrs. Dorcas Pimm examined it in May. It was not pretty. She took one end, gave Hetty Marlow the other, and they pulled. Nothing gave. “You could lead a horse with it,” Dorcas said, and Ned went red to the ears, never having had a finer compliment.

volumes.title: The Matter of the Red
volumes.text:
Clemency and Prudence Voss, sisters, of Mill Lane in Emberwick, had not spoken since a disagreement over damson jam eleven years before. They sat at opposite ends of the Tuesday Thimbles’ table, and each undertook one of the twelve quilts promised to Brindle House. Clemency’s was the fourth, all stars. Prudence’s was the fifth, all baskets.

Both patterns wanted red. There was one bolt of red flannel in the town, on the top shelf of Pimm’s the draper’s, and Dorcas Pimm, who owned the shelf, cut it in half.

It was not enough. In June Prudence ran short by four basket handles. A paper of red scraps appeared at her place, unaddressed. A week later Clemency wanted three star points, and found a paper at hers. By midsummer both quilts were done, each held some of the other’s red, and the sisters had got as far as “Thank you.”

volumes.title: The Notice in the Window
volumes.text:
At midsummer Dorcas Pimm looked at the slate by her kitchen door. Five quilts were finished for Brindle House, where twelve children from the Northern Fells would lodge come the snow. Seven beds were bare, and five of her nine months were gone. The Tuesday Thimbles numbered five, and one of them was eighty-one.

Dorcas did not care to ask for help. She did it anyway. She put a card in the baker’s window: one square of cloth wanted from every house in Emberwick, a span each way.

They came in for a fortnight. The baker sent a corner of apron, slightly scorched. The constable sent uniform blue. There was ferry sail, the back of a lamplighter’s glove, and from the library a strip of green book-cloth. Eighty squares made the sixth quilt. The Thimbles called it the Town Quilt, and argued over whose square was whose until dark.

volumes.title: Wool from the Fells
volumes.text:
By July the Tuesday Thimbles of Emberwick had made six of the twelve quilts promised to Brindle House, and had nothing left to fill the seventh. A quilt is a top, a back, and a warm middle, and the town had been combed of old blankets.

The middle walked in on a Tuesday. Greta Howe, a shepherd’s wife from the Northern Fells, had come eleven miles down the drove road with a pack of washed fleece on her back. Her two children would be boarding at Brindle House. She had heard there were strangers sewing for them, and she did not like to be beholden.

She stayed three weeks, carded the wool, and pieced the seventh quilt herself, grey and white, in a fell pattern of crossing paths called Sheep Trod. Dorcas Pimm asked which child it was for. Greta said that was the point. She would not know.

volumes.title: Two Crooked Ones
volumes.text:
The eighth and ninth of the twelve quilts for Brindle House were made in August by the schoolchildren of Emberwick, who had heard that fell children were coming to lodge for the winter and had views about what a bed needed.

Ned Sorrel, the saddler’s apprentice and the youngest of the Tuesday Thimbles, was put in charge, being fifteen and therefore nearly one of them. He taught running stitch to twenty-three children. He confiscated one frog.

No two squares came out the same size. The seams wandered. One quilt had a pocket sewn on the front with a marble in it, because a boy named Arlo said you needed somewhere to keep things. The other had a sun with a face. Mrs. Dorcas Pimm looked them over for a minute. Then she took out not one stitch, bound the edges, and chalked a new number on her slate: three.

volumes.title: Sixty Years Unfinished
volumes.text:
In September Hetty Marlow, who was eighty-one and the oldest of the Tuesday Thimbles, asked Ned Sorrel to carry a chest down from her attic. The circle still owed three quilts of the twelve promised to the children’s lodging at Brindle House, and Hetty had remembered something.

Under the winter curtains lay a quilt top, pieced and never quilted: small pink and brown triangles in rows, like geese going over. Her mother had begun it the year Hetty married, and put it by when her eyes failed. That was sixty years ago. The needle was still in it.

The Thimbles quilted it in a week, all five, following pencil lines so faint that Clemency Voss had to read them out to her sister. Hetty sewed the last corner by touch. Her stitches were enormous. Her mother’s, beside them, were tiny. Dorcas Pimm said they looked very well together.

volumes.title: All Night at the Corn Hall
volumes.text:
October came in cold, and the Tuesday Thimbles of Emberwick had ten quilts finished and two beds at Brindle House bare. The shepherds were saying snow within the month. Dorcas Pimm stopped trusting to Tuesdays. She borrowed the Corn Hall, set up the frame, and sent Ned Sorrel round the town with a handbell.

Thirty-one people came. The baker brought buns at midnight. The constable, who could not sew, held the lamp where he was told. Around the frame sat the Voss sisters side by side, Hetty Marlow, Greta Howe down again from the Fells, and anybody who could find an inch of edge.

The quilt was small yellow diamonds on dark blue, a pattern called Marsh Lights. They put the last stitch in as the windows turned grey. Dorcas went home and chalked on her slate, with a hand that shook slightly: one. Then she slept until Wednesday.

volumes.title: The Crumb Quilt
volumes.text:
Eleven quilts lay in Dorcas Pimm’s parlour in Emberwick, and not a yard of cloth was left in the town for the twelfth. The fell children were due at Brindle House that week. Dorcas had promised a quilt for every bed, in public, and she sat among the eleven feeling the want of one.

It was Prudence Voss who looked under the table. Nine months of quilting had left a drift of offcuts there: corners of Dorcas’s dresses, Hetty’s blue and cream, Ned’s flour sack, red flannel, a scrap of constable. Nothing was bigger than a playing card.

The Tuesday Thimbles sewed them together as they came, with no pattern. Clemency Voss said it was the ugliest thing she had ever helped make, and her sister agreed with her out loud, which had not happened in eleven years. They finished it on the Friday. On the Saturday it snowed.

volumes.title: The Thirteenth Bed
volumes.text:
The twelve children from the Northern Fells reached Brindle House in Emberwick on a carrier’s cart in the first snow of November. Twelve iron beds stood ready, and on each lay a quilt made by the Tuesday Thimbles. Dorcas Pimm stood by the stove, pretending not to watch.

The children chose. A tall girl took Ember Steps. A boy found the pocket and the marble. Greta Howe’s daughter went straight to Sheep Trod, though nobody had told her. Her brother Pip, aged six and the smallest, took the crumb quilt, and spent the evening finding a bit of every other bed in it.

Dorcas was putting on her gloves when she passed the housekeeper’s room off the kitchen. Mrs. Bray’s bed had one grey blanket on it. Dorcas looked at it for some time. Then she sighed, took her gloves off, and felt in her pocket for a needle.

volumes.title: Casting On
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, the Grey Coast, September. Dear Linnet, your letter came by the carrier, only a little damp. You ask if I will teach you to knit, as your gran would have. I will go one better. I am seventy-four, my knee has put me ashore, and my nephew Davy has the Kittiwake now. I shall knit you a gansey, the coast jersey, in dark blue wool, one band of pattern a month, and write how it goes. Come next August and fetch it.

You shall work too. I enclose a yard of cod line. Most letters will bring a knot. This month, the reef knot: left over right and under, then right over left and under. If it sits lumpy you have made a granny and must begin again.

Weather: first frost on the drying nets, white as sugar. I cast on tonight. Your grandfather, Tam Garrow.

volumes.title: Your Gran’s Needles
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, October. Dear Linnet, the gansey is begun. A gansey is knitted in the round on five steel needles, with no seams. These needles were your gran’s. Bess wore the ends of them bright. I also use her knitting stick, a piece of applewood that tucks in my belt and steadies the needle, so one hand is free to shoo the cat.

I have done the ribbed hem, and above it, in purl stitches, two letters: L.G., for Linnet Garrow. Every gansey on this coast carries its owner’s letters. Left on the quay, it finds its way home.

Your knot is the figure of eight. Make a loop, pass the end behind the standing line, and bring it back through the loop. It stops a rope running out through a ring. Weather: three gales in a fortnight, boats hauled up, everybody cross. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: Isaac’s Rope
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, November. Dear Linnet, this month the first band of pattern went into your gansey, and it is a cable: six stitches crossed over one another every sixth round, so they twist like rope. It is for Isaac Thrale. He is eighty and has kept the ropewalk behind the chapel all his life. He walks backwards down that shed twisting hemp, forty times a day, and has never once looked over his shoulder. Every boat here hangs on his work.

So your knot is the bowline, the king of them. Make a small loop in the line. Bring the end up through it, round behind the standing part, and back down the loop. It makes an eye that will neither slip nor jam.

Weather: fog for nine days. I knit by the sound of the fog bell and count rounds on my fingers. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: Peg’s Diamonds
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, December. Dear Linnet, the second band of your gansey is a row of open diamonds in purl. We call it net mesh, and it is for Peg Cuddy. Peg mends the nets on the quay in all weathers, in mittens with no fingers, and finds a torn mesh faster than you read a line of print. She looked at my knitting and said my tension had gone slack since I came ashore. I have tightened it. One does not argue with Peg.

Your knot is hers: the sheet bend. Make a bight in one cord. Bring the other up through it, round the back of both parts, and tuck it under itself. Every mesh of every net on this coast is that knot.

Weather: snow lying on the shingle, which I have seen only four times. The gulls are walking in it looking offended. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: The Night of the Ladder
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, January. Dear Linnet, on the fourteenth it blew from the north-east, and at dusk five boats were in and the Kittiwake was not. She was mine thirty years; my nephew Davy has her now. I sat in the window with your gansey, because hands must do something, and knitted the third band. It is the ladder: two purl rungs, two plain, climbing. It is the harbour steps, where everybody waits.

Davy came in at nine with a split sail and a full hold, grinning like a fool. Afterwards I found I had dropped six stitches and knitted one rung twice. I picked up the six. The doubled rung I have left in. It is a true record.

Your knot: the clove hitch. Two turns round a post, the second crossing the first, the end tucked under the crossing. The Kittiwake is tied so tonight. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: A Tide Mark in Blue
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, February. Dear Linnet, you ask why your gansey has other people’s patterns and none of our own. On this coast each family keeps its bands. But your father went inland to be a clerk in Emberwick, and you were born beside a river, not a sea. So I am giving you the whole village instead: the ropemaker’s cable, the net mender’s diamonds, the harbour steps. This month, a band of moss stitch, one plain, one purl, for the shingle we all walk on.

I ran out of wool halfway up. Ada Brock, the spinner at Fell Foot, sent more, and it is a shade darker. There will be a faint line across you, like a tide mark. I rather like it.

Knot: the round turn and two half hitches, for making fast to a ring. Weather: still and cold, the sea like slate. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: Nan and the Cliff Path
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, March. Dear Linnet, your knitted square came safe. It is wider at one end, rather like a map of the Lowlands, and I have pinned it above the mantel where Peg Cuddy can admire it. Keep on. My first was worse, and I was older.

This month’s band on your gansey is the zigzag, plain stitches stepping left and then right. That is the cliff path, for Nan Pellow, our postwoman, who walks it to the coast road and back daily, six miles, in whatever is blowing. Every letter of yours has come along that path in her hands.

Your knot is the fisherman’s knot, for joining two lines. Tie an overhand knot in each end around the other line, and pull. They slide together and lock. Weather: wind. When the gulls sit on the chapel roof facing inland, we take the washing in. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: Room to Reach
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, April. Dear Linnet, the body of your gansey has reached the armholes, and here is the cleverest thing in it. Under each arm I am knitting a gusset: a diamond of extra stitches, widening, then narrowing. You would never notice it. Without it a jersey rides up each time you lift your arm; with it you may haul a net or reach for an apple and the hem stays put.

I think of my nephew Davy when I knit them. I watched him from the quay hauling pots hand over hand. A fisherman is mostly reach.

Your knot is the sheepshank, which shortens a rope without cutting it: fold the slack in three and drop a half hitch over each end. In fifty years I have needed it twice, but it is handsome. Weather: showers, and a rainbow on the harbour bar most afternoons. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: Hen’s Feet
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, May. Dear Linnet, across the chest of your gansey, where the best band goes, I have put your gran’s. Bess had a pattern of her own: small chevrons, three stitches wide. She called it hen’s feet. She knitted it into every gansey I wore for forty years and never wrote it down.

So I took the last one she made me out of the chest and sat in the doorway reading it stitch by stitch, with a pencil, like a man copying a letter. It took two evenings. Peg Cuddy, who mends the nets, went by twice and for once said nothing.

It is in now, twelve rows of it, and I think Bess would pass it. No new knot. Tie the eight you have, ten times each, with your eyes shut. Weather: a warm white sea fret every morning, gone by ten. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: The Old Men’s Bench
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, June. Dear Linnet, the shoulders of your gansey are joined, and there is no sewing in it. I hold the front and back needles side by side and knit one stitch from each together, casting off as I go. It leaves a ridge like the keel of an upturned boat. Then the neck, in rib, loose enough to go over your head and plaits.

These light evenings I knit on the bench outside the net loft with the other old men. Isaac Thrale the ropemaker says the neck is too wide. Old Jory Kell says too narrow. Neither has knitted a stitch, and I have told them so.

No knot this month, but a habit. Coil your line in even rings, with a twist of the wrist at each turn, and hang it up. Weather: calm for a week, and mackerel in the bay. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: Made to Be Mended
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, July. Dear Linnet, the sleeves are done, and so is your gansey. I knitted them downward, shoulder to wrist. Every gansey is made so. Cuffs wear first, and when yours do you snip one thread, unravel to sound wool, and knit the cuff again. A gansey is made expecting to be mended. I think well of anything built that way.

I have made the sleeves long. You are eleven and not finished growing. And above each cuff I have left one band plain, for a reason I will tell you when you come.

It is washed in rainwater and dried flat on the garden wall, with a stone on each corner and the cat in the middle. Take the carrier to the coast road on the first of August. Nan Pellow will walk you down the cliff path. Weather: thunder out at sea. Your grandfather, Tam.

volumes.title: The Plain Band
volumes.text:
Gull Staithe, August. Dear Linnet, you have been gone two days and the house is very tidy. I did not say enough on the quay, so here it is.

The gansey fits, with room for two more Augusts. Peg Cuddy looked you over and said “It’ll do,” which from Peg is a speech. You tied the Kittiwake to the ring with a clove hitch, and a second for luck, and Davy pretended not to see. You went out past the bar on a flat sea and hauled a pot, and the hem stayed put.

The plain band above the cuffs is yours. Every other band is somebody of mine. When you have a pattern of your own, knit it in there. Bess’s needles and her knitting stick are in this parcel. Weather: the first cold dawn, and frost soon on the nets. Cast on. Your grandfather, Tam Garrow.
